How to follow up on a quote, with emails to copy

You sent a quote and heard nothing. Here is when to follow up, what to write, and when to stop, written for contractors and service businesses.

Checked 2026-11-21. Menus in other products change, so a label may differ slightly on your screen.

Short answer: follow up two or three days after you send a quote, again about a week later, and once more shortly before the quote expires. Keep each email short and add something useful each time. Send up to three follow-ups, then one short closing note. There is no single correct rule: advice from different sources ranges from one day to five.

When to follow up on a quote

We found no study of follow-up timing for quotes, so the timing you read online is common practice, and much of it comes from software companies that sell to contractors. The advice does agree on a rough shape:

  1. Two or three days after sending. Some sources say sooner, within a day or two. Others say three to five business days for a larger job. Two or three days is a safe middle.
  2. About a week after the first follow-up. Give them room. Sending reminders every day or two feels pushy.
  3. Shortly before the quote expires. If your quote has an end date, that date is a good reason to write. It is a fact, not a nudge.

Then stop. Two or three follow-ups, spread over about two weeks, is a common limit. Past that, you are more likely to annoy than to win the job. If the customer asks you to check back next month, do that instead of following your own schedule.

What makes a follow-up work

  • Add something each time. A question answered, an option, a start date. "Just checking in" three times is easy to ignore.
  • Make the next step easy. Ask one thing: can I answer questions, or do you want to book a date?
  • Say how to reach you. Give your phone number as well as your email.
  • Keep it short. Four or five lines is plenty.

Four emails to copy

1. Checking it arrived (two or three days after)

Subject: Quote for [job] - did it arrive? Hi [name], I sent over a quote for [job] on [date] and wanted to make sure it reached you. If anything is unclear, or you would like me to change something, just reply or call me on [phone]. [your name]

2. Answering questions or offering options (about a week later)

Subject: Re: Quote for [job] Hi [name], Following up on the quote for [job]. A few people ask about [scope or timing], so I wanted to mention it up front. If the price is higher than you hoped, I can offer a smaller version or do the work in stages. Tell me what matters most and I will send a revised quote. I could start the week of [date]. Would you like me to hold a spot? [your name]

3. Before the quote expires

Subject: Your quote for [job] expires on [date] Hi [name], A quick note that the quote for [job] is good until [expiry date]. After that, I would need to check materials and my schedule before confirming the price. If you would like to go ahead, reply to this email and I will book you in. If you need more time or have questions, call me on [phone]. [your name]

4. A polite last one

Subject: Closing out your quote for [job] Hi [name], I have not heard back, so I will assume the timing is not right and stop following up on the quote for [job]. If things change, reply here or call me on [phone] and I will be glad to help. Thank you for considering us. [your name]

The last email closes the loop. It tells the customer you will stop writing, and it sometimes prompts a reply when the others did not.

What to do when they go quiet

  • Pick up the phone. For a bigger job, a short call settles what several emails cannot. If you would rather not surprise anyone, send a short text first and ask when suits them. Only text customers who have agreed to be texted.
  • Offer a smaller option. If price is the likely problem, do not just cut it. Offer a smaller scope, different materials or doing the work in phases, and check the new price still covers your costs.
  • Let go gracefully. After your last email, move the job off your active list. Leave the door open, and keep the quote on file. If they do come back, you will have the details to hand.

How contractors differ from sales teams

Much follow-up advice online is written for sales teams. A homeowner choosing a roofer or a plumber is in a different position.

  • They are comparing quotes. Homeowners often get two or three. Do not race to undercut. Make sure they understand what your price includes, because quotes that differ in scope or materials are hard to compare.
  • You have usually met them. If you already did a site visit, refer to it. "When I was at the house on Tuesday I noticed the back fence" is a better opener than a generic message, and it shows you paid attention.
  • Season matters. If someone asks about outdoor work in the off season, they may not need to decide yet. Ask when they hope to start and follow that date, not yours. In your busy season, tell them when you could start, because an open week is a real reason for them to answer, and a full calendar is a real reason to keep a price for a shorter time.
  • Being pushy costs you. Plain, helpful messages beat a hard sell.

One caution: do not state a deadline or a price rise you will not honor. A real expiry date is fair. A made-up one damages trust, and it can cause trouble with the customer's agreement or local consumer rules. This is not legal advice.

A few things to check before you send

  • Has the customer already answered? Look in your inbox and your phone first. A follow-up to someone who replied yesterday looks careless.
  • Is the quote still right? If material prices or your schedule have changed, say so now rather than after they accept.
  • Is the address right? A quote sent to an old email address will never get a reply, and no number of follow-ups will fix it. If you have a phone number, use it.
  • Are you writing to the person who decides? On a home job, it may be a couple. On a business job, it may be someone else in the office. Ask who else should see the quote.

Doing it every time

The hard part is not the wording. It is remembering who is due a follow-up, three weeks after a busy day. Keep a simple list of quotes with the date sent, or set a reminder when you send each one. Outlook can remind you, but it will not send the follow-up for you. Our guide on automating follow-up emails in Outlook shows what it can and cannot do.
